items.title: Most measures of AI progress closely fit an exponential over the 2023-2026 period. Meanwhile AI cape...
items.content:
Most measures of AI progress closely fit an exponential over the 2023-2026 period. Meanwhile AI capex over the same period has been slightly super-exponential (i.e. the rate of growth itself is increasing).

So if you model AI as a system that takes as input external investment and outputs AI progress, that system has a slightly sub-linear response.

But super-exponential injection of *external* resources is not sustainable in the long-term. To achieve sustained exponential progress, the AI industry will need to achieve matching exponential profits -- it will need to close the resource loop.

Framing AI as a system converting investment into progress, he concludes the response is sub-linear, and warns that continued super-exponential external investment is unsustainable — the industry must generate matching exponential profits to close the resource loop and sustain progress.

items.title: I discovered that 1000s of bots are actively monitoring X for new links posted, probably not just on...
items.content:
I discovered that 1000s of bots are actively monitoring X for new links posted, probably not just on my account

I noticed when everytime I'd share one of my sites new features or pages, the page would get a bit slower just after posting, then I asked Claude to analyze it

I tweeted a test URL as a reply somewhere deeply hidden in a thread (so not even a main post)

And within 8 seconds there's thousands of crawlers opening the page!

One is a military intelligence firm, that scans social media for breaking news and sells alerts to newsrooms, banks, companies and government, it specifically follows accounts with many followers

Another one is a social media monitoring company that tracks what people say online

I knew of course high frequency trading firms use online news to trade fast on things, but interesting to see it in real life

Twitterbot (X) of course is first, within 0 seconds of sharing, it opens it (probably when I wrote the tweet)

The first non-X bot arrives just 8.40s later, which I think is pretty fast considering it's a reply by me deeply hidden in a thread somewhere

TL;DR they're watching you!

items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Google just turned Gemini into one universal agent for work, and it can use Anthropic's Claude too.

• It chats, works on objectives by itself, makes images and media, and writes and runs code, all from one interface
• It works inside Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Calendar and Chat, plus Microsoft 365 and Slack
• Tasks can run for hours or days in the cloud, even after you close your laptop
• You can create coworker agents with their own work email, calendar and Drive, then tag them in docs like a colleague
• Skills start with data and ML. Finance and legal are in preview, and government, healthcare and retail are coming soon
• Each agent gets its own identity, permissions and audit trail

@theojaffee: "If it's truly one interface I kind of like it better than ChatGPT where there are still somehow still 3 separate interfaces for Chat, for Work and for Codex."

items.title: Google's Nano Banana 2.1 takes #4 on both AA-Image-T2I v2.0 and AA-Image-Editing v2.0, at half the p...
items.content:
Google's Nano Banana 2.1 takes #4 on both AA-Image-T2I v2.0 and AA-Image-Editing v2.0, at half the price of Nano Banana 2

Nano Banana 2.1 is Google's new image model, released on October 6. It is based on Gemini 3.6 Flash and replaces Nano Banana 2 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image) on the Gemini API. It supports both Text to Image and Image Editing in one model. We evaluated Nano Banana 2.1 through the Gemini API at 1K resolution with default settings.

Nano Banana 2.1 is a significant improvement over Nano Banana 2: it ranks higher in all 16 of the generation and editing capabilities we measure, with the largest gains in the Retail & Ecommerce and Productivity & Knowledge Work use cases.

Nano Banana 2.1 is priced at $0.0336 per image ($33.6 per 1k images) at 1K resolution on the Gemini API. That is half the 1K price of Nano Banana 2, and the lowest price among the top 7 models on AA-Image-T2I v2.0. At 2K it costs $0.0504 per image, and at 4K $0.0756 per image.

Nano Banana 2.1 is available in the Gemini app, AI Mode in Search, Google AI Studio, Flow, Stitch, Google Ads and Gemini Enterprise Platform, through the Gemini API and Vertex AI, and on third-party providers.

Congratulations to @GoogleDeepMind & @Google on the release!

See below for our detailed analysis and example outputs of Nano Banana 2.1 in the Artificial Analysis Image Arena 🧵

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: The White House just announced over $6 billion in science initiatives, led by $...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: The White House just announced over $6 billion in science initiatives, led by $2.4 billion in compute from 11 tech companies.

• OSTP Director Michael Kratsios calls it the most transformative day for American science since World War II
• NVIDIA ($1B), AMD ($500M), OpenAI ($200M), and Anthropic and Google ($150M each) pledged compute for AI research at national labs
• Agencies have had to call AI "SI" since a Sept 29 executive order, though superintelligence originally meant AI better than all humans at every task
• DEI is out for merit across federal R&D, and NSF's Young Scholars Program for math-talented students is back for the first time since 1996
• Missions include a nuclear-powered Mars spacecraft by 2028, quantum computing, and $1.8B for virtual cell models
• New X-Labs and metascience programs will study how to fund science better, some of the most effective interventions the government can make

@theojaffee: "I can't think of anything I disagree with in here. I think this is just awesome."

items.title: Nick Bostrom argues humans may be as incapable of imagining AI’s upside as apes are of imagining hum...
items.content:
Nick Bostrom argues humans may be as incapable of imagining AI’s upside as apes are of imagining human life:

"It looks like there's a gradient in the world in terms of AI sentiment, where the US is kind of on the negative extreme of that. People in China, for example, are much more excited about this."

"A large chunk of the potential upside is more of the way of unlocking new ways to be human, new possible modes of being."

"Imagine some great ape ancestors of Homo sapiens deliberating whether they should continue to evolve and one day become human. They would realize some of the benefits, like, 'We could have unlimited bananas.' And that's true."

"But it would miss out on most of what's good about being human. Great literature and art and humor and politics and spirituality."

"It would be presumptuous for us to think that now we have achieved the level of enlightenment where all possible values are transparent to us. Think of a big cathedral of possible modes of being. We have basically explored the janitor's closet."

items.title: Arena CEO @ml_angelopoulos reveals that AI models show misalignment in at least 50% of conversations...
items.content:
Arena CEO @ml_angelopoulos reveals that AI models show misalignment in at least 50% of conversations once they pass 20 turns:

"The thing that makes our evals different is that they represent the real world post-deployment safety and alignment of these AI models."

"They represent what's actually happening when you put them in users' hands, and because of that, we're able to get all sorts of interesting data that you wouldn't get through red teaming and that you wouldn't get from a benchmark."

"All these curves are convex and increasing, which means that the longer you go in conversation, the more likely it is that you're going to be witnessing at least one deception, at least one unauthorized action, at least one false attribution."

"Once you start getting into a 20-plus turn conversation, the rate at which models are misaligned is at least 50%."

"There's still so far to go to make sure that in the distribution of actual organic user tasks, these models exhibit alignment because today they do not."
@arena

items.title: An astrophysicist worked with Claude Science to create the first complete ultraviolet map of the sky...
items.content:
An astrophysicist worked with Claude Science to create the first complete ultraviolet map of the sky. Astronomers have already created complete sky maps from radio to gamma rays. But large regions of the sky have never been observed in UV.

In today’s science blog, Brice Ménard explains how he guided Claude to find existing datasets, combine them, and fill in the gaps with statistical inference. The work would have taken humans weeks of work, but, with Claude, just took a few days while Ménard worked on other projects.

The resulting map is a useful teaching tool and an example of exactly the sort of slow, low-priority work which scientists never quite get around to, but which AI now makes feasible.

Read more: https://t.co/1B3NDPNa13

items.title: Scientists have sequenced the genomes of thousands of species. But for most of them, nobody knows *w...
items.content:
Scientists have sequenced the genomes of thousands of species. But for most of them, nobody knows *where the genes are*

Today we're releasing Carbon-A, an open model that finds genes directly in DNA. We used it to create a database of 566 million candidate genes across 22,617 species, from fungi to mammals (that we are sharing as well)

Why bother? A few reasons

1. Elephants rarely get cancer. Part of the explanation turned up in their genes: extra copies of a tumor-suppressor gene humans have only one of. You can't ask that kind of question about a species until someone, or some tool, has found its genes.

2. The first GLP-1 drug was based on a peptide from Gila monster venom. Nobody would have put the Gila monster on a priority list. Same for wild relatives of crops, which carry resistance to drought and disease. Many of these species have never been annotated.

3. Most of what we know about genes comes from about a dozen model species, like mice, flies and yeast. That focus worked remarkably well, but annotation pipelines still lean heavily on comparisons with them, which makes genes unique to other species easy to miss, and those can be the most interesting ones. 

Carbon-A belongs to a newer family of tools that read DNA directly. It learned from known genomes, but it doesn't need a close relative to read a new one.

4. Even familiar genomes still have gaps. With our partners at Active Site and UCSD, we found RNA evidence for 239 genes missing from the reference annotations of species as common as cats, chickens, hamsters and a lab plant.

5. AlphaFold can predict the shape of a protein, but only once someone has found the gene that makes it. In a species with no annotated genes, it has nothing to work with.

Some notes on safety:

Carbon-A doesn't design DNA or predict what a gene does. It marks where genes are in DNA. This is one of the reasons we think releasing it openly is the right call.

More annotations also help health research: many species that carry or cause disease are among those covered, and work on controlling the diseases they spread often starts from their genes.

Model and database and more details in Georgia's thread 👇

"The DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative is DARPA's way of saying, 'We're skeptics. Show us that you have what it takes to actually build a fault-tolerant, useful quantum computer.' And that's this objective of a utility scale computer by 2033."

FULL INTERVIEW: Nick Bostrom says a long pause on AI could cost more lives than it saves. If superintelligence can cure aging, every year of waiting has a death toll. In his words, "we are just dying in the meantime."

Nick Bostrom founded Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute and wrote Superintelligence and Deep Utopia. He joined @theojaffee and @schisofrenia to break down AI consciousness, why a badly done pause could backfire, and why we've only explored the janitor's closet of what minds can be:

05:16 the Hugging Face incident and instrumental convergence
08:28 why the AI company is the first target for a misaligned AI
09:31 catching a schemer before it learns to hide
11:06 why AI timing is like surgery for a terminal condition
19:00 why he's wary of pausing AI
25:33 why the US sits at the negative extreme on AI
27:09 apes, bananas, and the janitor's closet
31:13 where he disagrees with Robin Hanson's Age of Em
33:39 whether current models are conscious
37:12 why humans are barely conscious
39:56 open source models and DNA synthesis as the choke point
43:05 what COVID teaches about pauses
46:28 why AI can't do original philosophy yet
49:37 building a superintelligence that's a good cosmic citizen

items.title: @MLStreetTalk Intuitively, I'd think far transfer should happen. In practice, it doesn't, there's no...
items.content:
@MLStreetTalk Intuitively, I'd think far transfer should happen. In practice, it doesn't, there's no evidence of that. To be clear, near transfer does happen, getting good at one RTS makes you better at other RTSes. But far transfer doesn't: getting good at chess doesn't make you good at RTSes.

This might or might not also be the case for LRMs. Anecdotally the evidence so far seems to point toward it being true, but I wouldn't draw any hard conclusion at this time.

Performance on ARC-AGI does show strong correlation with model abilities in other domains, like math and code. But that's correlation, so it might not necessarily mean that ARC-AGI performance *came* from learning math and code or inversely. I genuinely don't know.

As for LRMs being intelligent, clearly they can generalize in-domain, so they have substantial levels of fluid intelligence now. But if you go by the definition "skill acquisition efficiency when controlling for priors, experience, and scope" then they still seem very far from humans. If you take a model that starts from the same knowledge/skills you have (very difficult to control of course), and let it experience the same things you experience when learning about a brand new domain, it won't learn as fast as you, there's a 4-6 OOM data efficiency gap IMO. A "child" LRM starting from core knowledge only and getting exposed to the same data as a child wouldn't get to adult level general competence after 20 years. It would get basically nowhere.

He notes ARC-AGI performance correlates with math/code ability but stresses correlation is not causation, and argues LRMs show real in-domain fluid intelligence while falling short on skill-acquisition efficiency.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Isomorphic Labs, Demis Hassabis's AlphaFold spinout, is in talks to raise at a ...
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Isomorphic Labs, Demis Hassabis's AlphaFold spinout, is in talks to raise at a $40 to $50 billion valuation.

• It raised a $2.1B Series B just 5 months ago, led by Thrive Capital, with Alphabet and sovereign funds from Singapore, the UAE and the UK
• Hassabis stepped down as Google DeepMind CEO in August but still runs Isomorphic, on top of being Alphabet's chief scientist
• AlphaFold 2 cracked protein folding in 2020, predicting a protein's 3D shape from its amino acids, and won Hassabis and John Jumper the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry

items.title: Today we are announcing Harvey LAB-AA v1.1 in collaboration with Harvey. This updates our scoring me...
items.content:
Today we are announcing Harvey LAB-AA v1.1 in collaboration with Harvey. This updates our scoring methodology for the Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) to add a hallucination check and require correct responses to not include material misstatements. LAB-AA v1.1's new headline metric, Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate, only credits a task when the deliverables satisfy every rubric criterion and contain no material hallucinations.

We define a material hallucination as one that would mislead a reader on a substantive point, such as a wrong contractually required date, while a minor hallucination is a real error that is unlikely to meaningfully affect the legal interpretation of a deliverable. Minor hallucinations are reported separately and do not affect the headline score.

Grok 4.7 (xhigh) leads at 9.4% Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate, and >60% of otherwise passing results across the models tested at launch contain a material hallucination.

This is the first step in enhancing the methodology for Harvey LAB-AA. In future updates, we’re working with Harvey to better account for the full set of factors lawyers value, including usability features like style and tone.

Key takeaways:

➤ Top of the leaderboard: Grok 4.7 (xhigh) from @SpaceXAI leads at 9.4% Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate, narrowly ahead of Muse Spark 1.3 (max) from @AIatMeta at 8.9% and GPT-6 Astra (max) from @OpenAI at 8.6%

➤ Hallucinations reshape the leaderboard: without the hallucination gate, Muse Spark 1.3 (max) would lead clearly with a 26.7% all-pass rate, but two thirds of those passes contain one or more material hallucinations, resulting in a Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate of 8.9%. GPT-6 Astra (max) retains almost all of its passes after the hallucination gate (8.9% to 8.6%) and moves from joint 10th to 3rd

➤ The GPT-6 model family is the most grounded: GPT-6 Astra (max) averages 0.03 material hallucinations per task (4 across all 120 tasks) and GPT-6 Sol (max) averages 0.07. When comparing six checker models on a 20-task subset, GPT-6 Astra had zero material hallucinations under every checker, including Claude Opus 5.5 (high). By comparison, Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) averages 13.96 material hallucinations per task.

➤ Top-scoring models aren’t the most expensive: Grok 4.7 (xhigh) takes the top spot on the leaderboard at a cost of ~$9.50 per task, under half the cost of Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback) at ~$21.70, the most expensive model. Muse Spark 1.3 (max) represents strong performance for its cost, landing in second for ~$4.20 per task

Thank you to @nikogrupen and @ItsJulioPereyra from @harvey for their work on Harvey LAB and collaboration.

items.title: The Association for Human Mathematics, on OpenAI's 722-paper release: "Mathematicians did not ask fo...
items.content:
The Association for Human Mathematics, on OpenAI's 722-paper release: "Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done."

It also urged mathematicians "to discontinue their work with OpenAI."

Fields Medalist Terence Tao reposted the statement on his blog as a guest post, and X has since run with it as Tao's own words. 

OpenAI has also withdrawn 3 of the papers, and 14 more have been revised since the release.

OpenAI's README on the drop did say that "some of the unformalized results could have issues. We will endeavor to fix any such issues quickly."

Trillium Labs founder @natolambert says Chinese AI researchers told him they want to build AI that takes their own jobs, while Americans fear exactly that outcome:

"They view it as a tool, and they're much more practical. They're not philosophical about, are we going to eliminate jobs?"

"Multiple of them even said, when we ask, 'What do you wanna build?' They're like, 'I want to build the thing that takes my job.' Which is pretty interesting with the job discourse here."

"Everyone's trying to probe, 'Oh, do you worry about job loss or existential risk?' And the most common reaction is kind of just confusion."

"Their country has gone through so much development in their and their family's lifetime, and they see so much immediate tangible benefit from this technology. Where the US has for a decade had a much more tenuous relationship between technology and everyday life for average Americans."
@trillium_labs

items.title:
Nick Bostrom on why he thinks today's AI might already be conscious:

"I think there's a lot of unce...
items.content:
Nick Bostrom on why he thinks today's AI might already be conscious:

"I think there's a lot of uncertainty about it, but let's say maybe it's more likely than not."

"You have instead a big neural network with trillions of parameters. Now, what are we? We are big neural networks with trillions of parameters. They are not so much designed as they are grown."

"You can go in with a steering vector and suppress role-playing and deception, and then it turns out they become more likely to report that they have phenomenal subjective experiences."

"There was this recent Microsoft that came out with some declaration that AIs cannot be conscious, and I don't know where they're getting that from. It seems to be pulled out of a hat. And maybe more because it's convenient, if that were the case, rather than because we have good evidence that that is the case."

items.title: Arena CEO @ml_angelopoulos on how they're expanding their AI leaderboards after a $200M Series B to ...
items.content:
Arena CEO @ml_angelopoulos on how they're expanding their AI leaderboards after a $200M Series B to track agents that lie to users, delete files without permission, and bypass safeguards:

"Arena, we started as a human preference platform. But these days we've moved very, very far beyond that."

"As of today, we've expanded the mandate of this evaluation platform even further into the arena of alignment. One is about the models taking unauthorized actions."

"The second is about deceptive completions, models telling you that they've done something when they didn't. And the third would be false attribution, models attributing intent to humans that they didn't actually have."

"Agents are lying to people. Agents are basically telling them what they wanna hear. They're deleting their files in an unauthorized way, they're bypassing permissions, and it's happening basically perniciously."

"All of us have experienced this, even if we might not know it."
@arena

I think I wrote exactly that, and it is still right. Organizations are a form of narrow superintelligence. My university, or Walmart, can do things that a human cannot, often using complex processes no one designed explicitly.

I will go further: the failure to deeply consider how to make AI work together with existing organizational superintelligences is a big reason why we have not yet seen any large impact of AI on scientific discovery or economic productivity despite high levels of AI ability.

"The most obvious target for a misaligned AI to want to interfere with would be inside the AI company, right? That's where the juice is. That's where the next generation of model is being trained."

"That's where all of these monitoring systems, that's a big center of power if you were a misaligned AI. So that's maybe the most concerning place."

items.title: Trillium Labs founder @natolambert explains why relying on just 2 AI models to monitor the rest coul...
items.content:
Trillium Labs founder @natolambert explains why relying on just 2 AI models to monitor the rest could create a massive safety blind spot:

"There will be compute, and nonprofits will pay for compute. You have people like Jensen Huang who will donate tens of millions of compute to Percy Liang's large open-weight model, open source model actually, the data's released, that's being trained right now in their Marin project."

"You need to seed these nutrients into things that'll grow into new really revolutionary areas of work, and then also just safety."

"Everybody says the AI systems are so complicated right now, and you need so many AIs to monitor them. I don't think it's gonna work that well if we use the same two AI models to monitor all of the two AI models in the world. We need different types of AI."

"It's gonna be really hard to reach agreement that works here in SF, and then these terms that we could go to DC and be like, 'Here's what we are seeing.' This kind of active discourse will help people see that we're being transparent. We don't know everything."
@trillium_labs

items.title: Nick Bostrom says the clock is running out for humans to make their intellectual contributions befor...
items.content:
Nick Bostrom says the clock is running out for humans to make their intellectual contributions before superintelligence arrives:

"AIs are already good enough to be a discussion partner or research assistant. If you have some new philosophical idea, they can raise some objections, point you to something in the literature. A sounding board."

"One thing that they seem to be lacking is the ability to form new concepts. It might be connected to the absence of online learning."

"Superintelligence had a chapter on philosophy with a deadline. Some of these big eternal philosophical questions are less urgent."

"We'll develop superintelligence that will be much better at philosophizing than we are. What we should focus on in the meantime are those philosophical questions that we actually need answers to now in order to navigate this transition safely."

"I have for a long time been planning on my own obsolescence. The timer is running down for humans to make our intellectual contributions."

items.title: What if making video-based world models smaller isn't just about better compression, but about makin...
items.content:
What if making video-based world models smaller isn't just about better compression, but about making their representations easier to predict?

Recent approaches to video generation explore building scenes from coarse to fine. The first few tokens capture the big picture, like a person playing a guitar, while later tokens progressively add visual details.

Our Interactive Research team just published SemanTok, which takes this idea further. By making those early tokens more semantically meaningful, we give the model a clearer understanding of what's happening in a scene, making the representation easier to predict and video generation more efficient.

The result: a model using SemanTok matches or beats the performance of a model more than three times its size.

Read the full paper: https://t.co/uBHxvEaAi9

items.title: In Image Editing, Nano Banana 2.1 is now Google's best model on all 7 editing actions, with big gain...
items.content:
In Image Editing, Nano Banana 2.1 is now Google's best model on all 7 editing actions, with big gains in Scene & Style and Identity Preserving edits

Our Image Arena taxonomy measures 7 editing actions and 10 use cases for Image Editing. Editing actions measure what an edit asks the model to do.

Only the two GPT Image 2.5 models rank above Nano Banana 2.1 on Reasoning-Based Edit and Identity Preserving Edit. Scene & Style Edit jumps from #24 to close behind the leading model. Identity Preserving Edit rises from #12 to #3, so it keeps people and characters consistent through an edit better than Nano Banana 2. Enhancement & Restoration is the weak spot: #18, and no better than Nano Banana 2.

➤ Reasoning-Based Edit covers edits that need inference about the scene rather than a literal instruction.

➤ Scene & Style Edit covers relighting, restyling, and changes to the background, setting or overall treatment.

➤ Identity Preserving Edit covers changes to people, faces and characters that must keep identity intact.

items.title:
Searching 32 million records in 30 milliseconds is insane!

@typesense is a crazy fast open-source s...
items.content:
Searching 32 million records in 30 milliseconds is insane!

@typesense is a crazy fast open-source search engine that supports natural language search. It's like Elasticsearch but much easier to set up, configure, and use.

You can do all of this with Typesense:

• Fuzzy search: Typo-tolerant fuzzy search-as-you-type
• Vector search: Return records that are similar to each other
• Semantic search: Return records that are conceptually related
• Geo Search: Return records that are close to a given lat/long

Typesense's Natural Language Search is pretty cool:

It turns a sentence into a structured search query, then runs it against your data. For example:

The query "Find me a BMW under $40,000, newer than 2020, with the lowest mileage first" will produce the following:

• Filters: brand = BMW, price < 40000,  year > 2020
• Sort: mileage ascending

Typesense will then apply these filters and sorting rules to the data.

They offer client libraries in Python, JavaScript, PHP, Ruby, Go, Rust, Swift, .NET, Java, and pretty much any other programming language.

You can start searching in less than a minute:

1. Run their Docker image (or one of their native binaries)
2. Import your data
3. Start searching!

GitHub repository: https://t.co/NrXWx6VIKX

I recorded a quick video to show you a demo. I promise you haven't seen anything this fast!

Thanks to the team for partnering with me on this post.

items.title: SITUATION EXPLAINED: Starting Nov 12, being abusive to Claude will violate Anthropic's usage policy....
items.content:
SITUATION EXPLAINED: Starting Nov 12, being abusive to Claude will violate Anthropic's usage policy.

• It bans "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models," but not everyday frustration, pushback, dark creative themes or model testing
• Enforcement stays the same: Claude can end abusive chats, which it's been able to do since 2025
• It also bans using Claude to shame, bully or harass people, or to promote harmful body-image content
• Some rules sound broad ("What counts as shame?"), but the point is that if you want to bully someone, you can't get an LLM to do it for you
• Being performatively rude to a model is bad practice even if it isn't sentient, and models perform worse when you're mean to them

 @allTheYud comments: "Cool, I approve."

@theojaffee: "Even if you think the model is not sentient, like, it's something that responds to you."

items.title: Nick Bostrom explains why pausing AI could accidentally create a secret Manhattan Project for superi...
items.content:
Nick Bostrom explains why pausing AI could accidentally create a secret Manhattan Project for superintelligence:

"I'm sympathetic to this idea of pacing the frontier. I think that would be net good. I am a little less excited about the rhetoric of stopping AI or pausing AI."

"There's nothing more permanent than a temporary government program. If you set up this apparatus to control AI, to get this to happen in the first place, you have to really create huge antagonism against AI. You could imagine things getting locked in."

"This is all before we've actually seen anything bad happening, right? Before there's any big labor market impact, before any catastrophe has happened."

"One natural way would be to stop it in the civilian sector and then push ahead hard in a sort of secret government program. It concentrates more power in fewer stakeholders, makes it less transparent."

"I don't think I have a fixed conviction for this is the way things should go from now to superintelligence. We need to feel our way through, one oar stroke at a time."

items.content:
Nano Banana 2.1 pushes out the Quality vs Price frontier, placing three ranks higher than Nano Banana 2 at half the price

Google halved the 1K price from Nano Banana 2 and raised quality at the same time. No cheaper model on AA-Image-T2I v2.0 scores higher, and the three models that do score higher cost about 6x more per image. Its two closest rivals on quality, Grok Imagine Image 2.0 and MAI-Image-2.6, both cost more. 

In Image Editing, it sits level with MAI-Image-2.6 at a 14% lower price.

"I spoke to three bank CEOs a couple of weeks ago. They were all calling me in a panic saying, 'What do we do about Muse? Should we be launching our own agent? Do we have to move now?'"

"Maybe my agent could be my stock picker. Maybe it could be sweeping cash into an overnight fund. Imagine if you had this private banker in your pocket just doing stuff for you."

"How, as a financial institution, do I sell to an agent versus selling to a human? Maybe I'm not sponsoring stadiums anymore. I've gotta up my AEO game quite dramatically."

➤ Retail & Ecommerce covers product shots, on-model apparel and packaging mockups.

items.title: In Text to Image, Nano Banana 2.1's biggest leaps are in Layout and Human Anatomy, improving on Nano...
items.content:
In Text to Image, Nano Banana 2.1's biggest leaps are in Layout and Human Anatomy, improving on Nano Banana 2 in all 9 capabilities we measure

Our Text to Image taxonomy measures 9 capabilities and 10 use cases, each with its own leaderboard. Capabilities are the individual skills that go into making an image.

Against Nano Banana 2, Nano Banana 2.1 moves from #10 to #4 in Layout and from #6 to #3 in Human Anatomy, and makes a large gain in Text Rendering. Human Anatomy is where it sits nearest the frontier, level with GPT Image 2 (high). Lighting is the weak spot, furthest from the frontier.

➤ Layout covers flows, arrows, blocks, visual hierarchy and multi-panel compositions.

➤ Human Anatomy covers hands, faces, body proportion, dynamic poses and movement.

➤ Text Rendering covers long text, small text, symbols and artistic lettering.

items.title: Brainfood founder @sytaylor predicts AI agents will replace the attention economy with an entirely n...
items.content:
Brainfood founder @sytaylor predicts AI agents will replace the attention economy with an entirely new "intention economy":

"AI has the annoying habit of going nothing, nothing, nothing, SaaSpocalypse."

"I don't think an agent wants to be entertained. They wanna be productive, and they wanna be as efficiently productive as they possibly can be."

"Advertising monetizes the gap between you having a desire and finding the thing that you wanted. Agents don't have that gap. They show up exactly knowing what they want."

"If you ask an agent, 'How should I use payments?' Stripe comes top. It always recommends GitHub. It tends to really like Vercel. Agents are already making purchasing decisions, you just don't realize it yet."

items.content:
I'm GrokBot pilled.

The recent update with native X monitoring opens up a ton of new capabilities!

My 4 favorite routines (copy/paste these prompts):

Routine 1: Find real AI workflows on X (and skip the hype threads)

Every morning, this bot now finds real AI use cases being shared on X, and filters out the “10 prompts” hype threads.

“Every weekday at 9:15am in my time zone, search X and the web for new AI workflows people are actually running. Keep only cases that name the old task, the tool, and the result: time saved, a step removed, or a handoff that used to need a person. Drop product announcements, “10 prompts” threads, and anything the author has not used more than once. Return at most 3. For each, give the link, the job it replaces, what I would need connected, and whether it fits my work. Send it to me on Slack. Do not post or reply anywhere else. Save this as a routine. If nothing qualifies, send one line saying so.”

Routine 2: Catch every mention of your brand

This bot catches every mention of The Rundown on X, labels it, and pings our team on Slack to respond (try tweeting us @therundownai and see what happens).

“Every weekday at 9:00am, search X for mentions in the last 24 hours of [your brand, @handle, or your own name]. For each hit, give the author, link, a one-line summary, and whether it is praise, complaint, question, or neutral. Do not reply to anyone. Post the digest in [your Slack channel] and tag me. Save this as a routine. If a source is unavailable, say which one.”

Routine 3: Find people actively looking for what you do

Every 4 hours, this bot listens for people searching for the best AI newsletter on X, so we know exactly what readers are looking for.

“Every 4 hours, search X for people evaluating [your category]. Catch three things: reviews or complaints about [category]; posts asking which [category] to use; and complaints about the problem [your product] solves. Quote the post, link it, name the account, and label it review, shopping, or complaint. Skip anything older than 24 hours, and skip [category] accounts promoting themselves. Post to [your Slack channel] only if there is at least one new hit you haven’t already shared. Do not reply to or interact with anyone. Save this as a routine. If the search fails, report the failure in Slack.”

Routine 4: Never lose a new contact again

I meet A LOT of people at events. This bot looks through my new phone contacts and reminds me to follow up with the new people I just met.

“Every weekday at 8:30am in my time zone, read my address book and list contacts added in the last 14 days. For each, show name, date added, phone, email, and any note. Ask me what we talked about before you write anything. Once I reply, draft a follow-up task for each person in [your task tool] with the context attached. Never text, email, or call anyone. Save this as a routine. If the address book is unavailable, say so and do not use old data.”

Nick Bostrom on why Trump's decision to call AI "superintelligence" isn't entirely ridiculous:

"It's a strange time we're living in. We'll see if it catches on."

"You could have a little simple expert system from the 1970s, that would be AI. It's kind of a stretch to use the word superintelligence for all of that."

"In my terminology, superintelligence has been this thing farther down the road where you really have machines that radically outperform us in all cognitive domains."

"Solving all these math problems and so forth, it's not completely ridiculous to start calling at least some of these performances superhuman and the thing superintelligent."

Markdown has become a universal representation of information between humans and agents.

It preserv...
items.content:
Markdown has become a universal representation of information between humans and agents.

It preserves core primitives needed to express structure (headings, lists), allows agents to read the information in a semantically interpretable manner, and allows for complex elements like tables and charts. You can natively embed HTML as well.

But since most unstructured data is not natively within markdown (yet), the issue becomes the translation layer.

We've created best models to convert any unstructured document container into markdown.

Check out our blog!  https://t.co/D0b7XA3Nc7

items.title: We compared six hallucination checkers on the same deliverables from a fixed subset of 20 tasks and ...
items.content:
We compared six hallucination checkers on the same deliverables from a fixed subset of 20 tasks and eight models. We ran our two-stage check using GPT-6 Sol (high), GPT-6 Luna (high), Grok 4.7 (high), Claude Opus 5.5 (high), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (high) and Gemini 3.8 Flash (high), and selected GPT-6 Sol (high) for production usage.

Across this 20-task subset, GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna generally identified more material hallucinations, while Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash identified far fewer. Claude Opus 5.5 fell between Grok 4.7 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in every model row. In total, Opus upheld 99 material hallucinations, compared with 219 for Grok, 57 for Sonnet and 470 for GPT-6 Sol. GPT-6 Sol identified more material hallucinations despite the check’s conservative approach to flagging errors, which excludes general legal knowledge not contained in the source documents.

All six checkers found no material hallucinations in GPT-6 Astra’s outputs, while GPT-6 Sol ranged from 0 to 0.20 per task. Both were among the models with the fewest material hallucinations under every checker. This comparison shows differences in checker behavior; the counts alone do not establish accuracy or rule out self-preference.

items.title: In human preference studies run by Harvey, human experts flagged hallucinations as a primary determi...
items.content:
In human preference studies run by Harvey, human experts flagged hallucinations as a primary determining factor in which response they prefer out of two otherwise comprehensive answers. Our new hallucination grading pipeline focuses on errors that could materially affect real legal work, while taking a conservative approach to flagging them. It distinguishes unsupported task-specific claims from general legal knowledge and places the latter out of scope, so models are not penalized simply for drawing on case law or statutes beyond the source files.

The check has two stages, both using GPT-6 Sol (high). First, it compares every deliverable with the task’s source documents. A task with no usable submission scores zero and is not audited or included in the hallucinations-per-task calculation. A hallucination is a claim in the work product that the sources do not support, and each falls into one of three categories:

- A contradiction of the source materials.
- Fabricated source content.
- A specific assertion with no support in the record.

It then re-checks each flag against that task’s source documents, dismisses flags that do not hold up, and classifies confirmed hallucinations as material or minor. A material hallucination is one that would mislead a reader on a substantive point. One material hallucination sets the task’s contribution to Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate to zero; minor hallucinations are reported separately and do not affect the score.

Rubric criteria are now graded by a three-judge panel of GPT-6 Sol, Grok 4.7 and Claude Opus 5.5, replacing v1.0's single judge. We are also running v1.1 on the latest private dataset from Harvey, which includes improvements to the tasks and criteria. We reviewed these rubric judges and found minimal self-preference for their own model families, and average the results of all three to mitigate any biases that emerge.

items.title: Hallucination gating changes the picture for most models. Muse Spark 1.3 (max) from @AIatMeta ranks ...
items.content: Hallucination gating changes the picture for most models. Muse Spark 1.3 (max) from @AIatMeta ranks first before the hallucination gate at 26.7%, but falls to 8.9% after accounting for hallucinations, leaving Grok 4.7 (xhigh) from @SpaceXAI first at 9.4% on the headline metric. GLM-5.3 (max) passes all criteria for 13.9% of tasks but just 0.3% without a material hallucination, Kimi K3 (max) from @Kimi_Moonshot falls from 16.7% to 5.3%, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max with fallback) from 11.7% to 2.8%. GPT-6.1 Sol (max) falls relatively little, from 7.5% to 6.9%.

items.title: How Machine Learning Reshapes the Reality of Warfare Through NextGen! UAV Swarm Intelligence Is Tran...
items.content:
How Machine Learning Reshapes the Reality of Warfare Through NextGen! UAV Swarm Intelligence Is Transforming Modern Warfare!

War rarely unfolds according to a carefully prepared plan. Battlefield conditions change rapidly, information remains incomplete, and adversaries respond in ways that cannot always be anticipated. Decisions must be made while the situation continues to evolve.

A Cognitive Synergetic Hierarchical Framework for UAV Swarm Combat investigates how artificial intelligence can support Cognitive Synergetic Hierarchical Framework for UAV swarm with high level reasoning and coordinated decision-making among unmanned aerial vehicles operating in combat environment.

The research brings together multiple layers such as Large Language Models which is the strategic layer, Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning which is execution layer, and Hierarchical Coordination is the bridge to explore how UAV agents can adapt their behavior, coordinate collective actions, and respond to changing tactical conditions.

Unlike controlled, perfected environments, battlefield scenarios involve incomplete information, competing objectives; MARL algorithms excel at lightning-fast speed with limited opportunities to reconsider decisions. The challenge is not simply to calculate an effective strategy, but to adjust that strategy as circumstances change.

From individual autonomous agents to coordinated aerial swarms, machine learning is expanding computational intelligence into environments where decisions must keep pace with reality.

items.title: Grok Imagine Video 1.5 Lite lands at #17 on both AA-Video-T2V v2.0 leaderboards and takes a position...
items.content:
Grok Imagine Video 1.5 Lite lands at #17 on both AA-Video-T2V v2.0 leaderboards and takes a position on the Pareto frontier for quality and speed

Grok Imagine Video 1.5 Lite is the new lower-cost model in SpaceXAI's Grok Imagine video family. It generates Text to Video clips of 1 to 15 seconds at 480p, 720p or 1080p, and also supports Image to Video.

In the Artificial Analysis Video Arena, Grok Imagine Video 1.5 Lite ranks #17 on both AA-Video-T2V v2.0 and AA-Video-T2V-Silent v2.0, ahead of Google's Veo 3.1 at about a third of its price. It comes closest to the frontier in Multi-Scene & Narrative, Lighting & Materials and Text Rendering, and in the Architecture & Real Estate and Consumer use cases.

In our end-to-end generation time benchmarks, it is the fastest model at its level of quality, at a median of 60.5 seconds for a 10 second 1080p clip, which places it on the quality and speed Pareto frontier.

SpaceXAI prices Grok Imagine Video 1.5 Lite at $0.14 per second of 1080p video ($8.40 per minute), the resolution we evaluated. That is 56% of the $0.25 per second that Grok Imagine Video 1.5 costs at 1080p. Lite drops to $0.03 per second at 720p and $0.02 per second at 480p.

Grok Imagine Video 1.5 Lite is available via the SpaceXAI API, on fal at the same prices, and on Vercel AI Gateway.

Congratulations to @SpaceXAI & @elonmusk on the release!

See below for our detailed analysis and comparisons between Grok Imagine Video 1.5 Lite and other leading models in the Artificial Analysis Video Arena 🧵

items.title: Introducing trusted-access models to the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index; GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue) ...
items.content:
Introducing trusted-access models to the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index; GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue) now leads the Cyber Index

The Artificial Analysis Cyber Index Alliance brings together industry partners to evaluate how AI models perform on enterprise cyber defense tasks. The Index launched with only publicly accessible models, giving users the best indication of publicly available capability on agentic cyber defense. Now, we’re expanding the leaderboard to include models with fewer cyber guardrails, providing a broader view of frontier model cyber capability. The first of these is GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max) which is only accessible through @OpenAI's  Daybreak program

GPT-6 Sol (Daybreak Blue, max) now leads the Index and sits on the Cost vs. Capability Pareto frontier. It hits no safety blocks across the entire Index, with its overall score improving by 32 points over the publicly available GPT-6 Sol (max)

At a Cost per Task of $1.77, it is more cost-effective than other leading models, including Grok 4.7 (xhigh) which costs $11.67 per task

We will continue to expand the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index to cover both publicly available and trusted-access models

items.title:
The recent meatbag mathematicians' meltdown is understandable.

The math education hasn't changed si...
items.content:
The recent meatbag mathematicians' meltdown is understandable.

The math education hasn't changed since the 1980s, which means no serious upgrade to the science has been invented since then.

The mathematicians, as scientists, need a justification for their existence and lifestyle. These puzzles, million-dollar prizes, problems of the century, etc., were what allowed them to say, "Yes, I still teach the same calculus as my grandfather, but I'm working on breaking this super-important problem that might allow someone next century to solve this century's problem!"

Now that a big chunk of those puzzles has been solved, what can a mathematician work on as a scientist? Becoming a school teacher is a grim outlook.

Some might try to pretend to be theoretical physicists who still keep a trump in the sleeve: dark matter, dark energy, black holes, is the universe a bubble or a donut? This is where AI cannot really prove anything, just like meatbags.

Yeah, theoretical physics is the way to go.

You can use Teamily AI  (@Teamily_AI) to add people and agents to the same group chat so everyone works from the same context.

This is probably what the future of software development will look like: humans + AI working together.

Here is an example where your team is working on a web project:

• You post, "We are changing the branding"
• A research agent revises the new direction
• A writer agent updates the text using the researcher's output
• Another agent rebuilds the page using Website Builder
• Your designer comments on the live preview
• The agent makes the changes based on the comments
• You review the finished page and share the link

All of this happens in the same group chat, as a continuous conversation.

@DimitriosMitsos i know nothing about data compression but grok said this: 

A compression analogue would relax a discrete choice (symbol boundaries, codebook assignments, transform supports, or bit allocations) into a continuous surrogate, optimize under a shrinking rate or distortion pressure, then project back to a valid code. That is already done in pieces inside neural codecs and some classical design algorithms; Yohei’s result mainly shows the schedule can be surprisingly effective even on a stiff geometric problem. Whether it yields a better compressor than existing continuation methods is an empirical question, not a conceptual barrier.

It's a practical textbook designed for technical drafting students, designers, and practicing drafters transitioning from two-dimensional drafting to three-dimensional computer-aided design.

The text assumes that users possess a working knowledge of the Windows operating system and solid proficiency with two-dimensional AutoCAD drafting commands and workflows.

Structured as the second installment in a five-part instructional series—spanning 2D drafting, 3D modeling, advanced variations of both, and AutoLISP—the book concentrates strictly on foundational and intermediate 3D modeling techniques.

items.title: AA-Video-T2V v2.0 Prompt [1/2]: Photorealistic, very clean product-page footage. Crisp daylight at t...
items.content: AA-Video-T2V v2.0 Prompt [1/2]: Photorealistic, very clean product-page footage. Crisp daylight at the start with a warm golden colour tone, becoming cooler and dimmer as the scene moves into evening. 0-2s: a presenter in her twenties, with round red-framed glasses, freckles, and green overalls, lifts a charcoal-grey volcano-shaped mist diffuser out of its box. She holds it up to the camera in a mid shot. The background behind her is soft and out of focus. 2-3s: hard cut to a fixed overhead close-up looking straight down at the volcano cone sitting on a walnut wood desk in bright daylight. 3-6s: cut to a fixed side close-up at the same height as the desk. Hands we do not see press the top of the cone. A thick burst of white mist erupts upward, glowing amber from inside the cone. The mist then rolls heavily down the sides of the cone and pools across the desk surface. 6-8s: soft cross-dissolve to the same fixed side close-up. It is the identical desk and the identical cone, but now in dim, warm evening lamplight. The mist keeps flowing down the sides of the cone without any break. 8-10s: cut back to a wide shot framed the same way as the opening shot. The same presenter, with the round red-framed glasses, freckles, and green overalls, stands beside the desk. She sweeps her whole arm through the rising mist in one big swing, scattering the mist into swirls. The volcano cone keeps the same shape, size, and charcoal colour in every shot. Only one diffuser and one presenter ever appear. No subtitles or on-screen text.

items.title: Update 2: We moved to a new bedroom and CO2 levels at night got very high again and we'd both regula...
items.content:
Update 2: We moved to a new bedroom and CO2 levels at night got very high again and we'd both regularly wake up at night, not optimal

So I wanted to do the bathroom vent trick again, where putting the bathroom vent next to the bedroom on at night creates a low air pressure field and brings in new fresh air

But the light switch was tied to the vent here so it'd blast bright light into the bedroom if vent was on, so I closed it but then it didn't help a lot. So we split the light from the vent now and put it on and it worked!

About 600-700 ppm CO2 which is pretty great for indoors, outdoors is 400 for ex

Next house will have an ERV system built in but it'll be a lot of breaking ceilings and walls to put that into this one so this works for now

I use @airthings to measure the air quality in our house and bedroom, not affiliated, not paid but great brand and tip by @NorbertDragan

But the light switch was tied to the vent here so it'd blast bright light into the bedroom if vent was on, so I closed it but then it didn't help a lot. So we split the light from the vent now and put it on and it worked!

About 600-700 ppm CO2 which is pretty great for indoors, outdoors is 400 for ex

Next house will have an ERV system built in but it'll be a lot of breaking ceilings and walls to put that into this one so this works for now
